issues.legal_issue: A stay of execution of a decree imposing reciprocal obligations to pay purchase money and deliver possession suspends the decree-holder’s obligation to pay while the stay remains in force.
material_facts: A pre-emption decree required the decree-holder to deposit the purchase money and the opposing parties to deliver possession upon deposit.
The opposing parties obtained a stay of execution before the deposit deadline.
The decree-holder deposited the money after the stated deadline while the stay was in force.
issues.conclusion: The stay suspended the whole procedure under the decree, including the decree-holder’s obligation to deposit the money, for as long as the stay continued.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 20, rule 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the obligations to pay the purchase money and deliver possession are reciprocal and interlinked. When a stay relieves one side of its obligation, the other side is correspondingly relieved of its obligation during the stay.

predicates.preemption_decree_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a decree granting pre-emption.
predicates.decree_links_payment_to_possession: The decree requires payment of purchase money in return for delivery of possession.
predicates.opposing_party_obtained_execution_stay: The opposing party obtained a stay of execution of the decree.

issues.definition: When a pre-emption decree links payment to delivery of possession and the opposing party obtains a stay of execution, the payment duty is suspended while the stay remains in force.

issues.legal_issue: When a final appellate court dismisses an appeal and confirms a conditional decree after the original payment deadline has expired, its decision may imply a fresh starting point for compliance with the payment condition.
material_facts: The decree required the decree-holder to deposit the purchase money by a specified deadline, after which the suit would stand dismissed.
The opposing parties’ second appeal was dismissed and the pre-emption decree was confirmed after the original payment deadline had passed.
The decree-holder had deposited the purchase money before the final appellate decision.
The courts below rejected the opposing parties’ application for restitution, but the High Court allowed it on the ground that the decree-holder had defaulted.
issues.conclusion: The final appellate decision implied a fresh starting point for depositing the purchase money; because the decree-holder had deposited it before that decision, there was no default, and the restitution application was to be dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 20, rule 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure, where the time fixed for payment has expired during an appeal, a final appellate court’s dismissal of the appeal and confirmation of the decree may, by necessary implication, extend the time and provide a fresh starting point. The Court approved Satwaji Balajiray Deshamukh v. Sakharlal Atmaramshet, I.L.R. 39 Bom. 175, and Sita v. Ramnath, I.L.R. 28 Patna 371.

predicates.conditional_preemption_decree_appeal: An appeal concerns a pre-emption decree that makes payment a condition of obtaining possession.
predicates.payment_deadline_expired_during_appeal: The payment deadline fixed by the decree passed while the appeal was pending.
predicates.final_appellate_court_dismissed_appeal_a: The final appellate court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the conditional decree.

issues.definition: When a payment deadline under a conditional pre-emption decree expires during an appeal and the final appellate court dismisses the appeal while confirming the decree, its decision implies a fresh starting point for payment.
